comment.value:
This paper presents EgoBlind, the large-scale egocentric VideoQA dataset for real-world visual assistance to blind individuals, comprising 1,392 videos and 5,311 questions collected and verified with participation from the blind community, and benchmarks across 16 MLLMs. 

It received 5 Accept ratings. Reviewers praise the dataset’s novelty, real-world grounding, high-quality question design, comprehensive benchmarking, and societal relevance. Concerns included dataset bias toward Chinese content, lack of certain ablations, absence of comparisons with task-specific systems, and limited blind-user involvement in some annotation stages. The authors provided thorough rebuttals and new experiments, which addressed most concerns to the reviewers’ satisfaction. 

Overall, given its technical soundness, strong impact potential, and careful ethical handling, the AC recommends acceptance. For the camera-ready, the authors should include promised additional analyses, improved documentation, responsible-use terms, and extended qualitative examples/code.
Thank you very much for all the constructive feedback. We will carefully incorporate the suggested enhancements into the final version.

Thanks for the kind reply and recognizing our continued efforts. We provide our further answers below and look for more positive opinions.

2. “… content creators are still selectively choosing what to film …”

We agree that it is unavoidable, but in our opinion it is not a major dataset issue. Instead, the selection may even help to limit redundant or tedious content and also help reduce privacy concerns.

3. “Will visually impaired users be involved in reviewing each data sample, or only a subset of them?”

We had 30% of the questions ( L.175, p.5) checked by visually impaired users.  This amounts to 1.5k unique questions; each question was surveyed amongst 10 to 33 blind users to ensure their relevance. The resulting observations (questions that blind individuals tend to ask or not in similar scenarios, see Supp. Sec. A.2) were then propagated to the entire dataset by the authors.  Note that the 30% subset already covers a variety of visual scenarios including housekeeping, shopping, transportation, outdoor activities, social gatherings, etc. 

4. “… unreliable evaluation …”

We consider GPT-4o mini’s evaluation more reliable than Gemini Flash-Lite because we manually finetuned its prompts to better align with human judgment (see L.263, p.6, and Supp. Sec. B.1). As the evaluation prompt does not need to generalize across models, we believe the evaluation is reliable, though not perfect. Currently, there is no standardized way to evaluate open-form answers, and the GPT score is widely accepted by the community.

Thanks for the kind reply and suggestions. We provide further answers below, and  hope they will mitigate the concerns and improve your opinion.

1. “Translate all questions to Chinese and see what the difference is …”

We translate the English questions into Chinese (via Google Translate API) and present results on a randomly selected half of the test samples due to time limitations. **All model performances drop by 1.5%~4.6%; so even though the data is collected in China, there is likely minimal data-to-language bias.**

We are grateful at your recognition of EgoBlind' novelty and significance, and appreciate the thoughtful and constructive feedback. Below we hope to address the major concerns.

W1. "When the ground truth answer is "I don't know" the camera wearer probably wants some further advice ... not included in the dataset."

Thanks for this suggestion.  In some questions, we did observe further suggestions following the ‘I don’t know’, but we did not especially restrict nor emphasize responses to reflect such live interactions and annotators were open in providing the response.  We appreciate the importance of such live and multi-round interactions for effective assistance and leave this for future work in new benchmarks.

W2. " does not account for the type of questions where the answer only comes some time after the question is raised (similar to the setting in VideoLLM-Online [1])."

Yes, thanks for the comment and the recommended work. In our current setting, if an answer comes after the question moment, it is answered based on the available visual content or with "I don’t know". This reflects the real situation and is different from  offline VideoQA. 

W3. "minor typos." 

Thanks a lot, we will fix such issues and further polish the writing.

**Additional questions and concerns**

Q1. "train/val split ... videos from the same content creator do not appear in both?" 

Thanks for the insightful point.  Originally, we only specified that video clips of the same video could not appear in both the train and validation sets.  We follow the suggested criteria of separating users to create a different split (half users in train and half users in val), and show the results below:
Method                     | Tool | Info | Navi | Safety | Comm | Res | Avg |  *Avg (ori, user-agnostic)*
:---------------------------|:----------:|:------:|:------:|:--------:|:------:|:-----:|:-----:| :-----:|
Qwen2.5-VL-7B (0-shot)        |   53.1   | 54.2 | 31.7 |  45.4  | 42.9 | 43.4 | 47.7 | *49.0*
Qwen2.5-VL-7B (finetune)     |   35.9   | 51.3 | 41.3 |  64.3  | 59.7 | 57.1 | 52.9 | *53.5*
InternVL2.5-8B (0-shot)          |   61.4   | 59.8 | 46.4 |  54.2  | 53.2 | 55.0 | 56.2 | *55.8*
InternVL2.5-8B (finetune)       |   55.5   | 59.0 | 57.9 |  69.9  | 62.3 | 71.4 | 62.3 | *62.1*


Fine-tuning improves Qwen2.5-VL and InternVL2.5 by 5.2% (vs. ori 4.5%) and 6.1% (vs. ori 6.3%)  respectively under this user-aware setting. The results and improvements are close to that of a user-agonostic setting (refer to Tab. 7 and Supp. Tab. 10). We speculate the reasons are two folds: 
- Although the videos may from the same user, the framed contents are different.
- The questions are posed by third participants and reflect their varied visual focus, even though the videos may from the same user.

We will add such results and analyses in the appendix of the final version.

Q2. "... exclusively recorded in China and most of the subtitles are also in Chinese...  analysis on how many of these questions can be answered just by visual cues and how many of the questions can only be answered with good Chinese understanding ability ...  give the LLMs which are trained on more Chinese data advantage?" 

Thanks for the comments.  We sample 10% of test data and invited people outside China (via the Prolific platform) to answer and mark the questions that they cannot answer due to Chinese-specific factors. The achieved accuracy is 90.0%, close to that of 87.4% by Chinese. Of 250 sampled questions (from users in Britain, Italy, US and South Korea), only 4 questions were marked as unanswerable because of Chinese-specific factors, indicating low rates of 1.6%. We speculate that the questions can be answered based on the accompanied contexts (English, icons, logos) most of the time, even though they do not know Chinese. 

As for evaluation bias towards ''Chinese-style'' models, Table 4 shows that GPT-4o and Gemini are the top 2; for open-source models, Qwen2.5-VL is well known for good Chinese reading capability, but its results are not outstanding.  

We will add such analyses to the final version.

Q3. "The dataset is provided but lacks proper documentation. No code is provided to reproduce the experiments in the paper?"

Thanks for highlighting this. we will improve the documentation for the camera-ready.  For code, we use off-the-shelf MLLMs and simply follow their protocols and APIs.  We will provide the finetuning code and scripts of the state-of-the-art open-source models (e.g., InternVL 2.5) together with the camera-ready.

We are grateful at your recognition of EgoBlind' significance and quality, and appreciate the thoughtful and constructive feedback. Below we hope to address the major concerns: 

1. "... may introduce bias because the content creators tend to be younger and more comfortable online, which does not represent the broader population of blind people."

We understand and appreciate the concern on data diversity.  Yet, we wish to highlight that the annotated questions reflect a wide range of blind people’s in-situation needs (ages 12 to 60, see Supp. Fig. 6), even if the visual contents are limited to content creators. We are working towards a larger and international extension of this dataset (refer to our answer to Q1 of **R-b8jE** for more details).

2. " Videos ... often picked or stylized." 

Thanks for the comment.  We shared similar concerns and addressed this during the video curation process by (1) excluding clips with strong indications of production and staging, (2) focusing on content creators whose aims were to video-log and promote the daily lives of the visual impaired.  We will make this clearer in the final version.

3. "Blind users played a limited role in question creation; most questions were generated by sighted annotators and only later verified by blind participants."

Thanks for the comment.  We wish to clarify that 15.4% of questions are posed by blind user themselves, while 84.6% of questions were generated by AI prompted to act as blind user. Sighted people were enrolled to quality check the questions, e.g. for redundancy and vision-irrelevant questions. Blind and visually impaired users were invited to check the questions’ relevance to their actual needs. We believe this is a reasonable and scalable way to collect questions and avoid contrived actions and questions from blind annotators.

4. " GPT-4o-mini to measure semantic similarity... which may favor models whose output style aligns with GPT-4o-mini’s language patterns."

Thanks for the comment. We carefully prompt GPT-4o-mini to focus on the semantic meaning instead of language pattern (refer to Supp. Table 10 for specific evaluation prompts). Importantly, we manually tune the evaluation prompts to make its judgements maximally align with human decisions. We also provide multiple reference answers. We believe these efforts effectively help limit the evaluation bias, especially those resulted from different language patterns. 

Additionally, we experiment with Gemini 2.5 Flash-Lite as evaluator with the same evaluation prompts. We report the average accuracy on a random half test samples and compare with that of GPT-4o mini. The results show the same performance tendency among models, though the absolute values vary (we did not tune the prompts for Gemini 2.5 Flash-Lite to align with human). We will extend the experiment to enclose more models, and add related analyses in the final version.
Method                     | Gemini 2.5 Flash-Lite (Evaluator)   | GPT-4o mini (Evaluator)
:---------------------------|:----------:|:------:
InternVL2.5-26B         |   56.1  | 54.6 
Gemini 2.5 Flash         |   64.6   | 54.8 
GPT-4o                       |   66.2   | 59.4 

5. " couldn't load all other files."

The dataset is large (80G) and we provide a google drive link in the download section of the README page. We also provide the evaluation script and attach the official code links of the MLLMs used in Table 4. We will release the fine-tuning code soon.

6. " demographic backgrounds of the video providers." 

Thanks for the suggestion. We will try to provide such information by checking the original video pages and contacting the providers if necessary.

We are grateful at your recognition of EgoBlind' novelty and significance, and appreciate the thoughtful and constructive feedback. Below, we address the major concerns.  

1. "All video clips originate from Chinese-language creators...  Broader sourcing would improve generalizability."

Thanks for the kind suggestion.  We appreciate the concern and agree that a broader geographic sourcing is more ideal.  Our initial search efforts when curating the videos did not lead to many suitable ego-view videos outside of Chinese platforms.  However, we are working towards an international expansion of this dataset through collaboration with relevant visual support associates in Asia, Europe and the US. 

Additionally, we wish to emphasize that **the broad QA contents are culture- and location-agnostic and should generalize** (refer to our answer to Q2 of **R-8Ksj**). Furthermore, even there are Chinese scene texts sometimes, the questions are answerable from corresponding image contexts (e.g., icons and logos) most of the time.

2. "Table 4 benchmarks sample frames from the entire video rather than restricting input to frames available up to each question timestamp." 

We wish to clarify that we **do follow a streaming protocol, so all results in Table 4 are based on the video content up to the question timestamp** (please see L.274~275 on page 7).

3. "Many videos contain Chinese subtitles or other on-screen text. MLLMs with strong OCR may extract answers directly from subtitles."

Thanks for highlighting this.  We believe that OCR, especially for on-screen text, does not play a significant role in supporting current answers (though we do find that most models are weak at OCR), because:
- according to our annotation experience, the subtitles are primarily irrelevant to the questions; an additional check of 250 random samples （~10% test data） shows that only 7 questions whose answers can be inferred from subtitles, with 2 prior to the question timestamp.
- video content is sampled only up to the question timestamp, which largely reduces the chance of answer leakage, since subtitles which may reveal answers tend to occur after this timestamp.
- even with strong OCR capability, e.g. Qwen2.5-VL, the performance on EgoBlind is still weak and not outstanding.  

4. "... video data is stored in the Google Drive, … make the data on Huggingface."

Thanks for the kind suggestion, we will check how to release the data (~80G) on Huggingface.

We are grateful for the recognition of EgoBlind' novelty and significance, and appreciate the thoughtful and constructive feedback. Below, we address the major concerns.  

1. "The benchmark ... lacks detailed analysis of specific failure modes... spatial reasoning, temporal reasoning, hallucination and misalignment... limits deeper understanding of where and why the model fails."

Thanks for this point and highlighting these possible failure modes. They are common with MLLMs and also arise in our benchmark, as the analysis in our paper shows: 
- understanding true user intention (often linked to user's historical activities or hand motions, i.e. **temporal context** and eye gaze, i.e. **spatial focus**) to support the interpretation of deictic words in the questions that are otherwise ambiguous (e.g., 'it', 'that', 'this').  Please see Fig.4a and Supp. Fig.14c.
- reasoning on the **spatial** orientation from **temporal** frames. Please see Fig.4b.
- providing reliable answers, which is related to **hallucination** and **misalignment** with users’ real-time visual environments (Fig.4d and Supp. Fig.14a).

The models often fail short in addressing the above challenges to answer related questions. Additionally, the detailed studies in Sec. B.3.1 at the supplementary show that questions of "Navigation", "Tool Use", and "Communication" require more temporal capabilities, while "information reading" questions rely more on spatial reasoning on a single frame. Thus, one can infer the models' capabilities based on their behavior across different question categories. 

We will enrich such analyses in the final paper.

2. "The evaluation focuses only on general-purpose MLLMs ... [no] comparison against any task-specific or rule-based visual assistance systems (screen reader, object detectors, OCR-based approaches) ... contextualize the performance of MLLMs within the broader assistive technology landscape."

Thanks for this feedback. We mainly test general-purpose MLLMs because EgoBlind targets a broader aspect of helping the visually impaired rather than a specific type of assistance (scene texts or object recognition). Task-specific or rule-based approaches could perform well on a certain type of questions, but we believe general-purpose MLLMs have their overall superiority towards in-the-wild assistance on a broader category of questions. We kindly wish to compare with specific assistance systems as future work, as they are out of our current scope.  

3. "An ablation study on prompt variation across different question categories (e.g., safety, navigation, tool use) ... navigation-related questions might benefit from spatially grounded prompts ... tool-use questions could require instruction prompts."

Thanks for the suggestion. We reflect the idea and design task-specific prompt for each question category, and assess the best open-source and closed-source models on 100 randomly selected samples for each category (if available, otherwise all samples of that category are used).  Table 1 shows that the task-specific prompts benefit GPT-4o's performance but slightly lower the performance of InternVL2.5. We speculate the open-source models are not strong enough to understand long and more complicated prompts. We will extend the analysis to more MLLMs in the final supplementary.

summary.value: This paper introduces EgoBlind, the first egocentric (first-person perspective) video-based Visual Question Answering (Video QA) dataset designed to support and evaluate visual assistance for blind individuals. EgoBlind comprises 1,392 videos recorded by real blind users and 5,311 questions, directly reflecting the visual assistance needs of the blind community. Using this dataset, the authors benchmark 16 SoTA multimodal large language models and find that even the best GPT model achieves only around 60% accuracy, which falls far short of human performance. The study reveals that current models struggle particularly with real-world support tasks such as navigation, safety warning, and tool use, and frequently fail to understand user context or intent.

strengths_contributions.value:
1. The paper introduces EgoBlind, which is the first large-scale egocentric Video QA dataset built entirely from first-person video captured by real-blind individuals. This real-world grounding significantly enhances the authenticity and relevance of the data, addressing a critical gap in the VQA and assistive AI research field.

2. The dataset features over 5,000 diverse, context-rich questions that are either directly posed or rigorously verified by blind users. These questions span practical assistive needs (such as navigation, safety, and using tools) ensuring the dataset faithfully reflects the real-world challenges blind individuals face in dynamic environment

3. By evaluating 16 state-of-the-art MLLMs (Including GPT-4o and Gemini the largest MLLMs), the study uncovers substantial performance gaps compared to human baselines and identifies key failure modes (poor spatial reasoning, sycophancy). These insights provide a valuable roadmap for advancing multimodal models toward more reliable and human aligned visual assistance.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
1. The benchmark reports overall accuracy and average score across question types, but lacks detailed analysis of specific failure modes. For example, spatial reasoning, temporal reasoning, hallucination and misalignment). This limits deeper understanding of where and why the model fails

2. The evaluation focuses only on general-purpose MLLMs, but does not have comparison against any task-specific or rule-based visual assistance systems (screen reader, object detectors, OCR-based approaches). This makes it difficult to contextualize the performance of MLLMs within the broader assistive technology landscape.

3. An ablation study on prompt variation across different question categories (e.g., safety, navigation, tool use) would provide deeper insight into how task-specific instructions affect model performance. For example, navigation-related questions might benefit from spatially grounded prompts (e.g., Guide the user based on their current position), whereas tool-use questions could require instruction prompts (e.g., explain how to operate the object the user is touching)

summary.value: This paper proposes an egocentric video question answering dataset specifically designed for scenarios involving individuals with visual impairments. This dataset emphasizes real-time QA by anchoring each question to a specific timestamp, simulating live visual assistance needs. The dataset includes questions posed or verified by blind individuals, enhancing its practical relevance. The paper also benchmarks a wide range of multimodal large language models (MLLMs), analyzing their performance across different assistive question types.

strengths_contributions.value:
1. The source of the dataset is new. The authors put efforts into crawling some new video sources and curate the questions both with GPT and human efforts.   
2. The dataset focuses on video QA for people with visual disabilities, which may have a further impact.    
3. Questions are posed or verified by blind volunteers; each has time-stamp alignment and ~3 independent reference answers, reducing subjectivity and enabling real-time evaluation.   
4. Videos (with creator consent), code, prompts, and evaluation scripts are publicly released, facilitating benchmarking and follow-on research.  
5. The QA pairs are well designed for different scenarios.   
6. 16 state-of-the-art MLLMs (open + closed source) are evaluated.  
7. Detailed error analysis pinpoints user-intention reasoning, spatio-temporal orientation, and reliability as bottlenecks, guiding future model design.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
- (***This is the major weakness from my perspective***) All video clips originate from Chinese-language creators, i.e., Bilibili, TikTok (Chinese version after manually checking the data), limiting cultural coverage and reducing the dataset’s relevance for non-Mandarin blind communities. Broader sourcing (YouTube, Instagram Reels, English/Spanish/Arabic content, etc.) would improve generalizability.  
- Table 4 benchmarks sample frames from the entire video rather than restricting input to frames available up to each question timestamp. This weakens the “real-time assistive” premise and inflates performance. A tighter protocol—e.g., camera-stream mode (see [Chatgpt Live Vision Feature](https://community.openai.com/t/acesss-to-openais-chatgpt-live-vision-feature/1053848) or strict windowed sampling—would better reflect on-device constraints.  
- Many videos contain Chinese subtitles or other on-screen text. MLLMs with strong OCR may extract answers directly from subtitles.

ethical_considerations.value: No, there are no or only very minor ethics concerns

dataset_code_comments.value:
The data (QA pairs, video data) and evaluation code are well provided. 
The only concern is that the video data is stored in the Google Drive, which might not be easy to download. For example, if the user wants to use the API to download Google Drive file, there will be some issue like the rate limit. Suggesting the user to make the data on Huggingface.

final_justification.value:
- My major concern is that the dataset comes from Chinese-only video content creators. However, the author addresses concerns with external experiments and explanation. 
- I also acknowledge the importance of an ego-centric dataset for blind people. So this work is valuable.

summary.value: This work introduces EgoBlind, a real-world egocentric video QA dataset collected from the perspective of blind users. Its goal is to evaluate how well multimodal large language models  can assist people with visual impairments. The dataset consists of video clips created by blind content creators, paired with questions that reflect their everyday needs. These questions come from six different topics which cover daily life. The authors employ a three-stage data collection and validation pipeline and benchmark 16 multimodal models. Results reveal a significant gap between model and human performance.

strengths_contributions.value:
1. The study uses first-person videos recorded by blind users to enable real-time assistance, tackling a socially important problem that could benefit many people.
2. The dataset is high quality. All video clips are collected by blind content creators, ensuring the scenarios genuinely reflect daily life for people with visual impairments.
3. The author benchmark the dataset comprehensively. They evaluate 16 multimodal large language models, both open-source and commercial.
4. Their analysis exposes current limitations of MLLMs and points to promising directions for future research.
5. Clear logical structure, easy to follow

limitations_weaknesses.value:
1. The data collection method may introduce bias because the content creators tend to be younger and more comfortable online, which does not represent the broader population of blind people
2. Videos posted by blind creators are often picked or stylized and may not accurately reflect their everyday experiences.
3. Blind users played a limited role in question creation; most questions were generated by sighted annotators and only later verified by blind participants.
4. The evaluation relies on GPT-4o-mini to measure semantic similarity, which may favor models whose output style aligns with GPT-4o-mini’s language patterns.

summary.value: The paper creates EgoBlind, a video question-answering benchmark that focus on real-world visual assistance for the blind people. Unlike most existing general Video QA datasets and benchmarks the paper features videos recorded by real visually impaired people (by collecting the videos posted by verified visually impaired content creators in online video platforms). The videos are then manually partitioned and edited. The questions are generated with a combination of transcription from the original video, generation from GPT-4o, and proposals from real blind people, and manually edited and verified by both sighted and blind people for correctness and relevance. Evaluation experiments with 15 open-source and closed-source MLLMs show that existing state-of-the-art MLLMs still performs a lot worse than humans on this benchmark, and could generate unreliable or malicious responses in some scenarios.

strengths_contributions.value:
- S1. Visual assistance for the blind is an important application of MLLMs, and EgoBlind presents one of the first large scale datasets in this domain. The experiments and analysis in the paper demonstrated that EgoBlind is different from existing Egocentric Video QA datasets and contains questions specifically designed for the purpose of assisting visually-impaired people. Therefore I found the paper to have good novelty and significance. 
- S2. The relationship of the work with existing datasets are clearly discussed. The paper is well-written and easy to follow. The figures, table, and captions are informative.
- S3. The authors properly discussed the potential negative social impacts and ethical concerns such as privacy issues regarding the use of videos collected from visually impaired content creators online.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
- W1. When the ground truth answer is "I don't know," the camera wearer probably wants some further advice on what to do so that the model can better answer the question, but this part of not included in the dataset.
- W2. Related to the point above, it seems that the dataset does not account for the type of questions where the answer only comes some time after the question is raised (similar to the setting in VideoLLM-Online [1]).
- W3. There are some minor typos in the paper. E.g. line 45 "three modes" should probably be "three models" and lines 313-315 the order of "2)" and "3)" are flipped.

[1] VideoLLM-online: Online Video Large Language Model for Streaming Video (CVPR 2024) https://arxiv.org/pdf/2406.11816

Additional questions and concerns:
- Q1. When doing the train/val split, did you make sure that the videos from the same content creator do not appear in both sets? Videos from the same content creator could often have similar themes, places, styles of subtitles, etc., leading to increased performance on the test set after fine-tuning on the dev set.
- Q2. It seems that the videos in the dataset are exclusively recorded in China and most of the subtitles are also in Chinese. It also seems that correctly answering some of the questions requires a precise understanding of the signs or marks that are in Chinese. Do you have an analysis on how many of these questions can be answered just by visual cues and how many of the questions can only be answered with good Chinese understanding ability (e.g. what is the human performance for someone who cannot read Chinese)? This might also bias the evaluation a little bit and give the LLMs which are trained on more Chinese data some advantage, and the authors should probably discuss this in the paper.

ethical_considerations.value: No, there are no or only very minor ethics concerns

dataset_code_comments.value: The dataset is provided but lacks proper documentation. No code is provided to reproduce the experiments in the paper.

final_justification.value: The authors made their best effort to address many of my concerns and most issues (W3, Q1, Q2) were resolved. While it would be more helpful to include answers that appear after the question in the video or provide the user with additional instructions when the answer is not available, I found the current version of the benchmark still adds considerable value to the community towards building better models for assistance to the blind and egocentric video understanding. I recommend acceptance and raised my confidence score.

title.value: EgoBlind: Towards Egocentric Visual Assistance for the Blind

abstract.value:
We present EgoBlind, the first egocentric VideoQA dataset collected from blind individuals to evaluate the assistive capabilities of contemporary multimodal large language models (MLLMs). EgoBlind comprises 1,392 first-person videos from the daily lives of blind and visually impaired individuals. It also features 5,311 questions directly posed or verified by the blind to reflect their in-situation needs for visual assistance. Each question has an average of 3 manually annotated reference answers to reduce subjectiveness.
Using EgoBlind, we comprehensively evaluate 16 advanced MLLMs and find that all models struggle.  The best performers achieve an accuracy near 60\%, which is far behind human performance of 87.4\%. To guide future advancements, we identify and summarize major limitations of existing MLLMs in egocentric visual assistance for the blind and explore heuristic solutions for improvement. With these efforts, we hope that EgoBlind will serve as a foundation for developing effective AI assistants to enhance the independence of the blind and visually impaired. Data and code are available at \url{https://github.com/doc-doc/EgoBlind}.
